title: Counts and Poisson regression
objectives: Model trade counts with Poisson regression and an exposure offset.

screens.title: Busy or quiet
screens.prose: 120 intervals of one stock: its volatility $v$ and the trades in each interval. Calm stretches were 30- or 60-minute intervals; volatile ones were 5- or 15-minute intervals. Fit the curve to the counts, then switch to trades per minute and fit again.

frames.caption: Each count divided by its interval length in minutes.

screens.question: Does volatility raise or lower trading activity?

options.text: It raises it: per minute, volatile intervals trade faster. Their counts are low only because they are short
It lowers it: the count curve slopes down
options.why: The counts mix interval lengths. A 5-minute count is small however busy the market is.

options.text: Neither: the two fits cancel out
options.why: They do not cancel. Per minute the rate clearly rises with volatility.

feedback.correct: Counts fall with $v$ only because the volatile intervals are short. The rate rises.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Switch to trades per minute and fit the curve there.

explain.text: Fitted to the counts the curve slopes down; fitted to the rates it slopes up. Interval length is tangled with volatility, so the count alone answers the wrong question.

screens.title: Put the interval length in the model
screens.prose: A count over $t$ minutes at rate $\lambda$ has mean $t\lambda$. With $\lambda = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1v}$, $\ln E[Y] = \ln t + \beta_0 + \beta_1v$. The term $\ln t$ enters with coefficient 1: an **offset**. The fit gives $\hat\beta_0 = -0.478593$ and $\hat\beta_1 = 0.059135$.
screens.question: By what factor does the trading rate multiply when volatility rises by 10 points?

byKey.lin: That is the change in $\ln\lambda$. The rate multiplies by its exponential.
byKey.one: That is one point of volatility. The step is 10 points.

explain.text: Ten points add 0.59135 to the log rate, so the rate multiplies by 1.8064. statsmodels with `offset=np.log(t)`, with `exposure=t`, and SciPy on the Poisson likelihood all give these coefficients.

screens.title: Expected trades in an interval
screens.prose: The fitted mean count in an interval of $t$ minutes is $\hat\mu = t\,e^{\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1v}$, with $\hat\beta_0 = -0.478593$ and $\hat\beta_1 = 0.059135$.
screens.question: How many trades does the model expect in a 15-minute interval at $v = 20$?

hints.text: Rate first, then times the minutes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the rate at $v = 20$ by 15 minutes.

byKey.rate: That is the rate per minute. The interval lasts 15 minutes.
byKey.hour: You used 60 minutes. The interval is 15.

explain.text: At $v = 20$ the rate is $e^{0.704106} = 2.0220$ trades a minute, so a 15-minute interval expects 30.33. The offset turns a rate model into a count model for any length.

screens.title: The Poisson likelihood with an offset
screens.prose: Derive the equations the fit solves, from the pmf $P(Y = y) = e^{-\mu}\mu^y/y!$, as in `estimation` lesson 7. One line drops the offset: leave it out.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $\ln P(Y_j = y_j) = y_j\ln\mu_j - \mu_j - \ln y_j!$, taking logs of the pmf
$\ln\mu_j = \ln t_j + \mathbf{x}_j^T\boldsymbol\beta$, the log link with the offset
$\ell = \sum_j [y_j\mathbf{x}_j^T\boldsymbol\beta - e^{\mathbf{x}_j^T\boldsymbol\beta} - \ln y_j!]$, the same likelihood for every interval length
lines.why: This line drops $\ln t_j$. It fits a rate as if every interval lasted one minute, which is the no-offset model.

hints.text: Start from one interval's log pmf.
Substitute the link with the offset before you differentiate.
Differentiate, then set the score to zero.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{X}^T(\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol\mu) = \mathbf{0}$ with $\mu_j = t_je^{\mathbf{x}_j^T\boldsymbol\beta}$: fitted trades match observed trades, column by column.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Log the pmf, put in the link with the offset, then differentiate.

byKey.x: You dropped the offset. Without $\ln t_j$ a 60-minute count is treated like a 5-minute one.

explain.text: The score has the same shape as the logistic one: $\mathbf{X}^T(\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol\mu)$. The offset sits inside $\mu_j$ and gets no coefficient of its own. The intercept's equation says the fit predicts all 7,125 trades.

screens.title: Is the coefficient on log time really 1
screens.prose: An offset fixes the coefficient of $\ln t$ at 1. To check that, fit $\ln t$ as an ordinary covariate. statsmodels gives it 0.976228 with SE 0.022235.

params.title: Poisson GLM with log t as a covariate

screens.question: What is the $z$-statistic for testing that this coefficient equals 1?

hints.text: Subtract the value under test, then divide by the SE.

feedback.correct: $z = -1.07$: the data agree with a coefficient of 1, so the offset is justified.

byKey.zero: That tests a coefficient of 0, as the summary prints. We are testing 1.
byKey.sign: Keep the sign: the estimate is below 1.

explain.text: $z = (0.976228 - 1)/0.022235 = -1.07$, well inside $\pm 1.96$. Counts grow in proportion to interval length, which is what an offset assumes.

screens.title: Leaving out the exposure
screens.prose: Fitting the counts without the offset gives $\hat\beta_1 = -0.020324$: a rate ratio of $e^{-0.20324} = 0.8161$ per 10 points. A colleague writes: "volatility lowers activity".
screens.question: What went wrong?

options.text: Short intervals are the volatile ones, so without the offset the slope picks up interval length
Nothing: the fit is the maximum likelihood estimate
options.why: It maximises the likelihood of a model with the wrong mean. The question was the rate, not the raw count.

options.text: Divide each count by $t$ and run OLS instead
options.why: That fixes the mean but treats a 5-minute rate as as reliable as a 60-minute one. A Poisson GLM with offset weights them properly.

options.text: Poisson regression cannot handle intervals of different lengths
options.why: It can, through the offset $\ln t$.

hints.text: Every interval with $v > 25$ lasted 5 or 15 minutes.
Without $\ln t$, the volatility slope absorbs the short intervals' small counts.

feedback.correct: The sign flipped because interval length was left out.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at how interval length lines up with volatility.

byKey.ok: You trusted the fit because it is an MLE. An MLE of the wrong model answers the wrong question.
byKey.ols: You divided by $t$, which fixes the mean, but OLS then weights a 5-minute rate like a 60-minute one.

explain.text: Without the offset the rate ratio is 0.8161 per 10 points; with it, 1.8064. This is your own slider fit from the first screen. A 5-minute rate has 12 times the variance of a 60-minute rate, so OLS on rates is noisy too.

screens.title: A quiet interval
screens.prose: None of our 120 intervals had zero trades. Suppose a 5-minute interval at $v = 20$ had none. A log transform could not use it; a Poisson model can. Its log-likelihood term is $y\ln\mu - \mu - \ln y!$.
screens.question: What is that interval's log-likelihood term, with the fitted coefficients?

hints.text: With $y = 0$, two of the three parts vanish.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $y = 0$ the term is $-\mu$.

byKey.rate: You used the rate per minute. The interval lasts 5 minutes, so $\mu = 10.11$.
byKey.pos: A log-likelihood term of a probability below 1 is negative.

explain.text: The term is $-\mu = -10.110$, so $P(Y = 0) = e^{-10.11}$, about 1 in 25,000. A zero is just a small count to a Poisson model. A log transform would have to drop it or add 1.

screens.title: Why not divide by time and use OLS
screens.prose:
For a count over $t$ minutes, $Y \sim$ Poisson$(t\lambda)$, so
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac{Y}{t}\right) = \frac{t\lambda}{t^2} = \frac{\lambda}{t}$$
Short intervals give noisy rates. The Poisson GLM with offset weights each interval by its information.
screens.question: At the same $\lambda$, how many times larger is the variance of a 5-minute rate than a 60-minute one?

feedback.correct: 12 times: the variance of a rate falls like $1/t$.

byKey.sd: That is the ratio of standard deviations, $\sqrt{12}$. The question asks for variances.
byKey.inv: You put the 60-minute variance on top.

explain.text: $\lambda/5$ against $\lambda/60$ is a ratio of 12. OLS on rates gives every interval equal weight; the GLM does not.

screens.title: Offset or exposure in statsmodels
screens.prose: statsmodels takes the interval length two ways: `offset=np.log(t)` or `exposure=t`, which it logs for you. The first run loads statsmodels, which takes 20 to 40 seconds.

params.title: statsmodels GLM, Poisson family, offset log t

screens.question: Complete `two_ways` so it returns both fits' `params`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm


def two_ways(X, y, t):
    """Return (params with offset=log t, params with exposure=t)."""
    ...
widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm


def two_ways(X, y, t):
    fam = sm.families.Poisson()
    a = sm.GLM(y, X, family=fam, offset=np.log(t)).fit()
    b = sm.GLM(y, X, family=fam, exposure=t).fit()
    return a.params, b.params

examples.setup: rng = np.random.default_rng(23); v = rng.uniform(10, 40, 120); t = np.where(v > 25, rng.choice([5, 15], 120), rng.choice([30, 60], 120)); y = rng.poisson(t * np.exp(-0.5 + 0.06 * v)); X = np.column_stack([np.ones(120), v])
examples.call: [round(v, 4) for v in two_ways(X, y, t)[0].tolist()]

screens.title: How fast to work an order
screens.prose: An execution model plans to trade no more than 10% of the market's prints. Volatility is now 30%. The fit says $\hat\lambda(v) = e^{-0.478593 + 0.059135v}$ trades a minute.
screens.question: How many trades does the model expect in the next 15 minutes?

feedback.correct: About 55 trades, so roughly 5 of our own prints fit inside the 10% cap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the rate at $v = 30$ by 15.

byKey.rate: That is trades per minute. The window is 15 minutes.

explain.text: At $v = 30$ the rate is 3.6527 a minute, so 54.79 trades in 15 minutes. A venue's fill rate is modelled the same way. Fills are a count over the time an order rests, with log time as the offset.

ideas: A count over $t$ minutes has mean $t\lambda$. Put $\ln t$ in as an offset, a term with coefficient fixed at 1.
With a log link, $e^{\Delta\beta}$ is a rate ratio: 10 points of volatility multiply trading by 1.8064.
Leaving out the offset flipped the volatility slope to $-0.020324$, because short intervals were the volatile ones.
summary.trap: Fitting counts over unequal intervals without the offset lets interval length masquerade as a covariate effect.

quiz.prose: In a Poisson model of trades, one interval lasted 30 minutes.
quiz.question: What is that interval's offset?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The offset is the natural log of the interval length.

byKey.raw: The offset is $\ln t$, not $t$. `exposure=t` takes the raw length.
byKey.log10: You took a base-10 log. GLM links use natural logs.

explain.text: $\ln E[Y] = \ln t + \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol\beta$, so the offset is $\ln 30 = 3.4012$.

quiz.prose: A Poisson model of daily fills has a coefficient of $-0.05$ on the spread in ticks.
quiz.question: What does one more tick of spread do to the expected fills?

options.why: You read the coefficient on the count scale. With a log link it acts on $\ln\mu$.
Close, but $e^{-0.05} = 0.9512$, a 4.88% fall. The 5% reading is the small-coefficient approximation.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Exponentiate the coefficient.

explain.text: With a log link, one more tick multiplies the mean by $e^{-0.05} = 0.9512$, a 4.88% fall.

quiz.prose: A model of fills per minute meets a minute with no fills.
quiz.question: How does a Poisson GLM treat that minute?

options.text: As an ordinary observation: its log-likelihood term is $-\mu$
It must be dropped, since $\ln 0$ is undefined
options.why: The link logs the mean, not the count. The count of 0 enters as $0 \cdot \ln\mu = 0$.
Adding 1 is the patch for log-transformed OLS. A Poisson model needs no patch.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the term $y\ln\mu - \mu - \ln y!$ at $y = 0$.

explain.text: At $y = 0$ the term is $-\mu$, perfectly defined. Zeros carry information about how quiet the market was.
